title: Solomon's knot
subtitle: An elongated loop locked with a slip stitch — the lace mesh stitch
excerpt: Solomon's knot is an elongated chain loop that is locked in place with a slip stitch through the back strand. Working pairs of these knots creates an airy, spider-web mesh that holds its shape without any foundation chain. One of the most elegant openwork structures in crochet.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), lace crochet chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Solomon's knot (also called lover's knot) is documented in Victorian needlework literature as a lace-mesh structure.
heroPrompt: A swatch of Solomon's knot mesh crochet in fine cream cotton thread, showing the open diamond-mesh created by the elongated knots, dramatic light showing the openwork structure.

glossaryTerms.definition: An elongated chain loop locked with a slip stitch through the long back strand. Pairs of these knots form a diamond mesh fabric without a traditional foundation chain. Also called lover's knot.

content.text: is a chain loop pulled tall — much taller than a normal chain — then locked through the back strand with a slip stitch. The locking slip stitch creates a knot midway along the elongated loop. Repeating this structure creates a diamond mesh fabric where every intersection is a locked knot rather than a worked stitch.
Yarn over and pull up a long loop — approximately 1.5 cm for DK yarn, longer for lace weight. Do not let it slip back down to normal chain size.
Yarn over and pull through the loop as a normal chain. The elongated loop now has a chain stitch at the top.

Look at the elongated loop. There is a back strand running along its length (the single strand at the back, separate from the front V). Insert the hook under this back strand, in the centre of the elongated loop.
Yarn over and pull through both the back strand and the hook loop in one move (a slip stitch). One loop remains. The knot is locked.

attrs.title: Consistency is everything
attrs.body: The mesh only works if every Solomon's knot is exactly the same length. Pull each loop to the same height before working the chain and locking slip stitch. Use a small ruler or a cut piece of card as a height guide until the tension is consistent.

content.text: Each row is a pair of Solomon's knots, then a dc into the locking point of the pair in the previous row. The pairing is what creates the diamond shape: two knots lean away from each other from the same dc base, and the dc of the next row sits at the meeting point of two pairs from below.

attrs.heading: Solomon's knot problems
attrs.intro: Three problems specific to Solomon's knot.

items.symptom: The mesh looks irregular with some diamonds larger than others
items.fix: Pull every elongated loop to exactly the same height before taking the chain stitch. Any size variation multiplies across the mesh.

items.symptom: The back strand cannot be found for the locking slip stitch
items.cause: The elongated loop was pulled so long that the back strand blends with the surrounding yarn.
items.fix: Work at a moderate length — 1-1.5 cm for DK. The back strand needs to be visible as a distinct bar before you lock it.

items.symptom: The locking slip stitch is too tight and pulls the loop out of shape
items.cause: The lock stitch was pulled through too firmly.
items.fix: Lock with a light pull. The locking stitch should hold the loop centre, not constrict it.

content.text: Solomon's knot shawls and bags are the natural first project. Fine cotton or linen yarn makes the mesh particularly dramatic. The mesh also works as a background for motifs — Irish crochet motifs are traditionally appliquéd onto a Solomon's knot ground.
